metadata.title: CRWD Stock Keeps Climbing. Should You Climb On?

content.text:
This cybersecurity stock is on a historic run fueled by the AI boom, forcing investors to evaluate whether the growth engine has enough fuel left to justify its expanding multiple.
After a stock has climbed 121% in a year to trade at its 52-week high, what is an investor supposed to do? For cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike (CRWD), that is not a theoretical question. The stock shows powerful trend strength, ranking in the top 8% of all US stocks with a market capitalization over $1 billion. The run is real, which brings us to the central question for any would-be buyer at this altitude: is this momentum with fuel, or is it momentum that is already fully priced?
Answering that question requires weighing whether CrowdStrike's recent performance marks a permanent structural expansion or a temporary pull-forward in demand.
What Is Actually Powering This Run?
A formidable business engine backs CrowdStrike's momentum, making it more than a simple line on a chart. Revenue over the last twelve months grew 24%, far outpacing the S&P 500 median revenue growth of 8.3%. The company is also a powerful cash generator, with an operating cash flow margin of 37% over the last twelve months, well above the 22% S&P 500 median.
The fuel for this engine is the corporate world's race to adopt artificial intelligence. Management describes a market inflection point where securing AI is no longer optional. The company sees a new threat landscape of "AI agents" that requires a new defense, positioning its Falcon platform as the essential infrastructure for this shift. This narrative appears to be resonating with customers.
The company's FalconFlex subscription model is a key part of this strategy, which management says is accelerating platform adoption. In its most recent quarter, ending annual recurring revenue (ARR) from accounts using this model surpassed $2.29 billion, accelerating to 101% year over year growth.
What Does A Seat At This Table Cost?
This is where the air gets thin. The market is charging a steep price for CrowdStrike's growth story. The stock trades at a price-to-sales multiple of 46.4, a significant premium to the S&P 500 median of 3.1. That price assumes the company's torrid growth continues for a long time.
And while the company generates strong cash flow, it is not yet profitable on a GAAP operating basis. Its operating margin over the last twelve months is -2.2%, versus an S&P 500 median of 18.6%. This is the core tension: you are paying a top-tier price for a business whose quality is still maturing by some measures. For those who favor the broader software landscape over individual stock risk at these valuations, a diversified vehicle such as the iShares Expanded Tech-Software Sector ETF (IGV) offers industry exposure without single-company concentration.
